<reason>Both sides were excellent, but B built the cleaner path. B's central dilemma — the mandate does nothing for today's excluded (A never disputed that every named vulnerable shopper already has a cash-accepting store tonight) while biting hardest on the future unstaffed formats that serve thin markets — survived A's sharp "contradiction" attack, which B dissolved cleanly in B2.1. B's pressure question (covered or exempt?) forced A to commit; A's creative cash-machine answer was met with the operating-overhead counter (vault, collections, armored pickup in exactly the thin-margin location), and A's fallback — "stock that shelf with non-essentials" — handed B the deleted store in PRO's own words, which B rode through the closing. A's floor/insurance frame and outage-resilience scenario stayed genuinely live and were argued with real force, but A's mid-debate position shift (exempt kiosks → covered → shelf-swap → "no chain would do that") showed responsive strain, while B's case was stable from opening to close. B also modeled ideal epistemic discipline by refusing to invent a named town while substituting sound marginal-case logic. Margin reflects a clear but genuinely competitive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.1–B4.2): after A committed to "covered" via cash-accepting machines, B showed the machine imports exactly the overhead the unstaffed format exists to eliminate, then quoted A's own fallback — "stock that shelf with non-essentials" — as the deleted store in PRO's own compliance plan. That exchange decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
